The Papuan mountain pigeon (Gymnophaps albertisii) is a relatively small columbid endemic to the montane forests of New Guinea. Newly hatched chicks, likely similar to the closely related stock dove (Columba oenas) in developmental trajectory, emerge from the egg at a very modest weight of 12 grams [Wwb = 12 grams]. This altricial nestling then undergoes a period of rapid growth within the nest, fed on crop milk by both parents. Following a typical Columbidae developmental schedule, the chick reaches the critical milestone of fledging, achieving its first flight, at 31 days after hatching [tx = 31 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This period of nest dependency is relatively short for a bird that will attain a much larger adult size. The species exhibits a marked sexual size dimorphism, with adult females reaching a considerably larger ultimate body mass. Field measurements of reproductively active adult females consistently record a maximum body weight of 259 grams [Wwi = 259 grams], a value that places Gymnophaps albertisii among the medium-sized members of its genus and reflects the energetic demands of egg production and incubation.

The reproductive biology of the Papuan mountain pigeon is characterized by a notably slow pace of life, typical of many tropical forest columbids. Females typically produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a conservative reproductive strategy that is common among pigeons. Furthermore, breeding events are not frequent; available data indicate that a female will raise just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This low annual fecundity is offset by a comparatively long lifespan and extended parental care. The initiation of this first reproductive effort, representing the time since birth at first brood, occurs relatively late in life. Observations of marked individuals in the wild suggest that birds do not attempt to breed until they are approximately 840 days since birth [tR = approximately 840 days since birth], a delay that underscores the extended period required to acquire the necessary foraging skills, establish a territory, and attain full physical maturity in the challenging monta at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]ne environment.

Under standard metabolic conditions at a core body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the basal oxygen consumption, representing the maximum basal metabolic rate, has been recorded at 170 milliliters per hour [JOi = 170 milliliters per hour]. This relatively moderate metabolic rate is consistent with the energy-sparing lifestyle of a frugivorous bird living in a cool, high-altitude habitat. The same thermal regime is critical for understanding the species' developmental biology. The age at birth, a period that encompasses the full incubation duration from laying to hatching, has been estimated at 16 days [ab = 16 days] when eggs are maintained at 40.5 °C at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This incubation period is comparable to that of other similar-sized pigeons and reflects the precise thermal requirements for successful embryonic development within the calcareous egg.

The species' life history is further distinguished by a delayed onset of sexual maturation. Young birds do not reach the stage of puberty until well into their first year of life. The time since birth at puberty has been determined to be 99 days [tp = 99 days] when raised under optimal conditions at a stable body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Following the attainment of puberty, there is a further significant interval before birds engage in their first breeding attempt, highlighting a conservative reproductive strategy that prioritizes survival and somatic growth over early reproduction. This combination of a late puberty and a delayed first brood contributes to a life-history strategy geared towards high adult survival in a relatively stable, albeit resource-poor, montane ecosystem where the risks of reproduction are high for inexperienced individuals. The long developmental period allows juveniles to thoroughly learn the locations of fruiting trees essential for survival.

Longevity data for the Papuan mountain pigeon indicate a remarkably extended lifespan for a bird of its body size. Field records and observations of banded individuals suggest that the maximum lifespan in the wild approaches 6,059 days [am = 6,059 days] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This extraordinary longevity, equivalent to over 16 years, is a hallmark of a "slow" life-history strategy characteristic of many tropical island and montane bird species that face low extrinsic mortality rates. This extended lifespan allows individuals numerous breeding opportunities across many years, partially compensating for the extremely low annual reproductive output of a single egg per year. The evolution of such a long life is likely linked to the species' frugivorous diet, which buffers against short-term food shortages, and the relative safety of its cloud forest habitat from many of the predators that threaten lowland congeners. Ultimately, this suite of life-history traits—low fecundity, delayed maturity, and exceptional longevity—defines the ecological niche of Gymnophaps albertisii in the ancient forests of New Guinea.
